questions.question: From which Roman emperor's reign, celebrated as the golden era of Virgil, Horace, and Ovid, did English writers of 1700–1745 derive the title 'Augustan Age'?
questions.explanation: Eighteenth-century writers compared their era of classical refinement to the Rome of Emperor Augustus.

questions.question: The boundaries of the Augustan Age (1700–1745) are traditionally marked by the death of John Dryden in 1700 and the deaths of which two major writers in 1744 and 1745?
questions.explanation: Pope died in May 1744 and Swift died in October 1745 closing the Augustan phase of Neoclassicism.

questions.question: Which publication, launched in London in March 1702 near Fleet Bridge, was the very first regular daily newspaper in England?
questions.explanation: The Daily Courant was first published on 11 March 1702 by Edward Mallet and soon managed by Samuel Buckley.

questions.question: Under which monarch was the Act of Union passed in 1707, formally uniting the kingdoms of England and Scotland into Great Britain?
questions.explanation: The Acts of Union took effect on 1 May 1707 during the reign of Queen Anne who ruled from 1702 to 1714.

questions.question: What landmark literary and legal principle was established for the first time by the Statute of Anne passed by Parliament in 1710?
options: Royal pensions for all university poets
Free postal delivery for literary journals
questions.explanation: The Statute of Anne 1710 granted authors legal copyright for fourteen years renewable for another fourteen.

questions.question: During which span of years did Alexander Pope, the central poetic figure of the Augustan Age, live?
questions.explanation: Alexander Pope was born in London in May 1688 and died at Twickenham in May 1744.

questions.question: Which four-part seasonal work, printed in Jacob Tonson's 'Poetical Miscellanies' in 1709, was Alexander Pope's first published poetry?
questions.explanation: Pope made his poetic debut in May 1709 with four Pastorals dedicated to the four seasons.

questions.question: Which 1713 topographical poem by Alexander Pope celebrates both the rural landscape of the Thames valley and the Tory Peace of Utrecht?
questions.explanation: Pope published Windsor-Forest in March 1713 combining landscape description with praise for the Treaty of Utrecht.

questions.question: How many cantos comprised the original 1712 version of Alexander Pope's 'The Rape of the Lock' before he expanded it to five cantos in 1714?
questions.explanation: The first version of The Rape of the Lock appeared in Lintot Miscellany in 1712 in two cantos of 334 lines.

questions.question: What is the name of the chief guardian sylph who warns Belinda of impending disaster in Alexander Pope's 'The Rape of the Lock'?
questions.explanation: Ariel visits Belinda in a morning dream in Canto I and leads the airy cohort of fifty sylphs.

questions.question: Which fashionable three-handed card game does Belinda play against the Baron at Hampton Court in Canto III of 'The Rape of the Lock'?
questions.explanation: Pope describes Belinda game of Ombre at Hampton Court as an epic battlefield of kings queens and knaves.

questions.question: Which 1717 Ovidian heroic epistle by Alexander Pope portrays a medieval nun torn between her religious vows and her passion for her former teacher?
options: Elegy to the Memory of an Unfortunate Lady
questions.explanation: Published in Pope 1717 Works Eloisa to Abelard dramatizes the tragic passion of Heloise in her convent cell.

questions.question: Which two classical Greek epics did Alexander Pope translate into heroic couplets between 1715 and 1726, earning a handsome fortune?
questions.explanation: Pope translated Homer Iliad from 1715 to 1720 and the Odyssey with Elijah Fenton and William Broome from 1725 to 1726.

questions.question: What famous subterranean ornamental feature, decorated with shells, mirrors, and crystals, did Alexander Pope build beneath his villa at Twickenham?
questions.explanation: Pope constructed his famous Twickenham grotto as an underground passage connecting his riverside lawn to his back garden.

questions.question: In which philosophical poem by Alexander Pope does the celebrated maxim 'Know then thyself, presume not God to scan; / The proper study of Mankind is Man' appear?
questions.explanation: These lines open Epistle II of Pope An Essay on Man published in 1733.

questions.question: Of which historic cathedral in Dublin was Jonathan Swift installed as Dean in 1713, serving there until his death in 1745?
questions.explanation: Queen Anne ministry appointed Swift Dean of St Patrick Cathedral Dublin in April 1713.

questions.question: To whom were Jonathan Swift's intimate daily letters written in London between 1710 and 1713, later published as 'Journal to Stella', primarily addressed?
questions.explanation: Swift wrote the Journal to Stella to Esther Johnson and her companion Rebecca Dingley in Dublin.

questions.question: In Part I of Jonathan Swift's 'Gulliver's Travels', what is the name of the empire inhabited by diminutive people barely six inches tall?
questions.explanation: Shipwrecked in his first voyage Gulliver wakes up bound by threads on the shore of Lilliput.

questions.question: In Part II of 'Gulliver's Travels', what is the name of the land inhabited by towering giants some sixty feet in height?
questions.explanation: In his second voyage Gulliver is left behind in Brobdingnag where a farmer girl named Glumdalclitch cares for him.

questions.question: Which neighboring island empire wages a bitter war against Lilliput over whether boiled eggs should be broken at the big end or the little end?
questions.explanation: Blefuscu represents Catholic France while the Big-Endians and Little-Endians satirize religious schisms.

questions.question: In Part IV of 'Gulliver's Travels', what name is given to the filthy, avaricious, and degenerate creatures who possess human form?
questions.explanation: The Yahoos are savage human-like brutes in Houyhnhnmland who embody human vice and unreason.

questions.question: Which pioneering thrice-weekly periodical did Daniel Defoe write almost single-handedly from 1704 to 1713 while supporting Robert Harley?
questions.explanation: Defoe launched A Review of the Affairs of France in February 1704 and continued it until June 1713.

questions.question: For which 1702 ironic pamphlet impersonating a High-Church Tory extremist was Daniel Defoe fined, imprisoned, and stood in the pillory?
options: Reasons Against the Succession of the House of Hanover
questions.explanation: Defoe anonymous 1702 hoax proposed hanging Dissenting preachers angering both Tories and Dissenters.

questions.question: Which 1722 work by Daniel Defoe presents a vivid, documentary-style narrative of the 1665 outbreak of bubonic plague in London?
options: A Journal of the Plague Year
questions.explanation: Published in March 1722 A Journal of the Plague Year reconstructs the terror and statistics of London in 1665.

questions.question: Which 1724 novel, Daniel Defoe's last major work of fiction, is subtitled 'The Fortunate Mistress' and follows a wealthy courtesan?
questions.explanation: Roxana or The Fortunate Mistress was published in 1724 depicting a high-society courtesan haunted by guilt.

questions.question: Which three-volume travel and economic work did Daniel Defoe publish between 1724 and 1726 describing the commerce and towns of Britain?
options: A Tour Thro' the Whole Island of Great Britain
A Plan of the English Commerce
questions.explanation: Defoe Tour provides a comprehensive account of early eighteenth-century British industry roads and towns.

questions.question: Which 1705 poem did Joseph Addison write at the request of Whig ministers to celebrate the Duke of Marlborough's victory at Blenheim?
questions.explanation: Addison The Campaign compared Marlborough to an angel riding a whirlwind and earned him a government post.

questions.question: Which 1713 neoclassical blank-verse tragedy by Joseph Addison dramatizes the final stand of a stoic Roman republican against Julius Caesar?
questions.explanation: Addison Cato was staged at Drury Lane in April 1713 and applauded by both Whigs and Tories as a hymn to liberty.

questions.question: On which three days of the week was Richard Steele's periodical 'The Tatler' published between 1709 and 1711?
questions.explanation: Steele issued The Tatler on Tuesday Thursday and Saturday to match the days the post left London for the country.

questions.question: Which devotional manual did Richard Steele publish in 1701 while serving as an ensign in the Coldstream Guards?
questions.explanation: Steele wrote The Christian Hero in 1701 arguing that true heroism requires Christian morality rather than Pagan stoicism.

questions.question: Which 1722 comedy by Richard Steele, featuring the virtuous Young Bevil and the orphan Indiana, is considered the masterpiece of early sentimental comedy?
questions.explanation: Adapted from Terence Andria Steele The Conscious Lovers sought to provoke tears of moral sympathy rather than coarse laughter.

questions.question: Which 1706 comedy by George Farquhar, set in the market town of Shrewsbury, portrays Captain Plume and Sergeant Kite enlisting soldiers?
questions.explanation: Farquhar drew on his own military recruitment duty in Shropshire to write The Recruiting Officer in 1706.

questions.question: Who are the two impoverished young gentlemen who pose as master and servant while fortune-hunting in Lichfield in Farquhar's 'The Beaux' Stratagem' (1707)?
questions.explanation: Thomas Aimwell and Francis Archer take turns acting as master and footman in Farquhar final masterpiece.

questions.question: Which kindly country gentlewoman in George Farquhar's 'The Beaux' Stratagem' gave her name to the English expression for a charitable patroness?
questions.explanation: Lady Bountiful cures her rural neighbors with herbal remedies and spends half her income on charity.

questions.question: Which dramatist and Poet Laureate published the first modern edited six-volume edition of William Shakespeare's plays in 1709?
questions.explanation: Nicholas Rowe 1709 edition added dramatis personae lists act-scene divisions stage directions and the first formal biography.

questions.question: What dramatic subgenre, focusing on the pathetic sufferings of a distressed or penitent woman, did Nicholas Rowe popularize in the early 1700s?
questions.explanation: Rowe coined the term she-tragedy in 1714 for plays like The Fair Penitent and The Tragedy of Jane Shore.

questions.question: Which unrepentant seducer in Nicholas Rowe's 1703 tragedy 'The Fair Penitent' gave his name to the standard English word for a heartless rake?
questions.explanation: The gay gallant Lothario who seduces Calista in Rowe The Fair Penitent became synonymous with a male seducer.

questions.question: Which 1716 mock-georgic poem in three books by John Gay offers witty advice on navigating the mud, pickpockets, and traffic of London?
options: Trivia: or, The Art of Walking the Streets of London
questions.explanation: Gay Trivia takes its title from the Roman goddess of crossroads and vividly depicts Augustan street life.

questions.question: What was the title of John Gay's 1729 sequel to 'The Beggar's Opera', set in the West Indies, which was banned from performance by the Lord Chamberlain?
questions.explanation: Walpole government suppressed the stage production of Polly in 1729 though Gay earned a fortune selling it by subscription.

questions.question: Which 1731 prose domestic tragedy by George Lillo portrays the apprentice George Barnwell being lured into theft and murder by Sarah Millwood?
questions.explanation: The London Merchant or the History of George Barnwell broke neoclassical convention by making a middle-class apprentice a tragic hero.

questions.question: Which Prime Minister pushed the Theatrical Licensing Act through Parliament in June 1737 to silence the stage satires of Henry Fielding?
questions.explanation: Provoked by Fielding Pasquin and The Historical Register for the Year 1736 Walpole instituted strict stage censorship.

questions.question: How did the passage of the Theatrical Licensing Act of 1737 directly transform the literary career of Henry Fielding?
options: He emigrated permanently to Dublin to manage the Smock Alley Theatre
He accepted a government sinecure as Poet Laureate under George II
It ended his career as a playwright and turned him toward the law and novel-writing
He abandoned secular writing to take holy orders in the Anglican Church
questions.explanation: Shut out of the theatre at the Little Theatre in the Haymarket Fielding entered the Middle Temple and soon began writing fiction.

questions.question: Which 1743 satirical biography by Henry Fielding equates the notorious London gang leader and thief-taker with Prime Minister Robert Walpole?
options: A Journey from This World to the Next
The Life of Mr. Jonathan Wild the Great
questions.explanation: Published in Volume III of Fielding Miscellanies in 1743 Jonathan Wild ironically praises ruthless villainy as Greatness.

questions.question: In Samuel Richardson's 1740 novel 'Pamela', who is the wealthy squire who attempts to seduce his deceased mother's virtuous maidservant before marrying her?
questions.explanation: Mr B of Bedfordshire and Lincolnshire is reformed by Pamela steadfast virtue and marries her in the second half of the novel.

questions.question: Which actor-manager and Poet Laureate published the lively theatrical memoir 'An Apology for the Life of Mr. Colley Cibber, Comedian' in 1740?
questions.explanation: Colley Cibber published his candid Apology in 1740 providing an invaluable history of the London stage since 1690.

questions.question: Which Augustan female poet published 'Miscellany Poems' in 1713 containing the sensitive nature lyric 'A Nocturnal Reverie'?
questions.explanation: Anne Finch Countess of Winchilsea was praised by William Wordsworth in 1815 for the fresh natural images of A Nocturnal Reverie.

questions.question: Which Augustan aristocrat and poet wrote a celebrated collection of letters describing Ottoman society during her husband's embassy to Constantinople (1716–1718)?
questions.explanation: Lady Mary Wortley Montagu recorded her travels in the Turkish Embassy Letters and introduced smallpox variolation to England.

questions.question: Which Irish bishop and philosopher published 'A Treatise Concerning the Principles of Human Knowledge' in 1710, advancing the idealist thesis that to be is to be perceived?
questions.explanation: George Berkeley Bishop of Cloyne formulated subjective idealism or immaterialism summed up as esse is percipi.

questions.question: Which Scottish Enlightenment philosopher published his foundational empiricist work 'A Treatise of Human Nature' in three books in 1739–1740?
questions.explanation: David Hume published Books I and II of A Treatise of Human Nature anonymously in 1739 and Book III on morals in 1740.

questions.question: Which Nonconformist minister published 'Hymns and Spiritual Songs' (1707) and 'The Psalms of David Imitated' (1719), earning the title 'Father of English Hymnody'?
questions.explanation: Isaac Watts composed classic hymns including Our God Our Help in Ages Past and When I Survey the Wondrous Cross.
